title_th: การสั่งฟาสต์ฟู้ด
recycles: numbers 1-100 and prices ('How much is it?')
polite requests: 'Can I get… please?' / 'Could I have…?'
clarification: 'Sorry, could you say that again?' / 'Did you say X or Y?'
yes/no answers and short confirmations: 'That's it, thanks.'
register: Casual-polite, fast and transactional (counter and drive-thru staff are friendly but rushed; first names are not used)

targets.why_it_matters_here: Thai finals are unreleased, so 'no ice' comes out as 'no eye' and the cashier hears nothing at all — you get a cup packed with ice. 'Large' without the /dʒ/ sounds like 'lar' and staff default to a small. At a drive-thru speaker there is no face to read and no time to repeat, so a dropped final consonant is a wrong order you pay for.

Teen/ty confusion here costs money and food: say 'combo thirteen' when you mean 'thirty' and you eat the wrong meal; hear 'fifteen' when the total is 'fifty' and you hand over the wrong cash at a queue that is already moving. Order numbers are called out once over a loud speaker — mishear 'thirty-two' as 'thirteen-two' and your food sits on the counter going cold.

model_dialogues.label: At the counter — a standard combo order

lines.speaker: Cashier
lines.text: Hi there, what can I get you?
lines.th: สวัสดีค่ะ รับอะไรดีคะ

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Can I get a chicken burger combo, please?
lines.th: ขอชุดเบอร์เกอร์ไก่หนึ่งชุดครับ

lines.text: Sure. Small, medium or large?
lines.th: ได้ค่ะ เอาไซซ์เล็ก กลาง หรือใหญ่คะ

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: A large combo, please. And no ice in the Coke.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: To go, please.

lines.th: 14.50 นะคะ คิวที่ 32 ค่ะ

lines.speaker: Customer

lines.th: ขอโทษครับ 32 หรือ 13 ครับ

lines.th: สาม-สอง ค่ะ สามสิบสอง เดี๋ยวเรียกนะคะ

lines.speaker: Customer

chunk_drills.label: Ordering by item or by number
chunk_drills.pattern: Can I get + (a / two) + [item OR number] + please
examples: Can I get a cheeseburger combo, please?
Can I get combo number three, please?
Can I get two number sixes, please?
Could I have six nuggets, please?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Recycles polite request 'Can I get… please?' from cafe_coffee_order, plus plural -s as an audible final consonant (sixes, nuggets, fries).

chunk_drills.label: Size and upsizing
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Recycles small/medium/large from drinks ordering; drills the final /dʒ/ in 'large' that Thai speakers drop.

chunk_drills.label: Customising your order
examples: Can I get the sauce on the side?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Negative determiner 'no + noun' (no article), contrasted with 'not' — 'No ice' NOT 'I don't want ice'.

chunk_drills.label: For here or to go
chunk_drills.pattern: For here / To go / It's takeaway
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Short answers to alternative questions; recycles 'please/thanks' politeness tags.

chunk_drills.label: Checking a number or a price
examples: Sorry, did you say thirteen or thirty?
Could you say the total again, please?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Recycles clarification questions from phone_call_basics; reported-speech opener 'did you say…' with rising-falling contrast on teen/ty.

listening_items.audio_text: That'll be thirteen twenty. Order number fifty.
listening_items.question: How much is the total, and what is the order number?
listening_items.distractor_focus: thirteen vs thirty; fifty vs fifteen

listening_items.audio_text: Sorry, the milkshake machine's down. Do you want a Coke instead?
listening_items.question: What can't you order, and what is offered instead?
listening_items.answer: No milkshake; a Coke is offered instead
listening_items.distractor_focus: final consonants in 'milkshake' and 'down' lost through speaker distortion

listening_items.audio_text: Is that for here or to go?
listening_items.question: What is the cashier asking?
listening_items.answer: Whether you are eating in the restaurant or taking the food away
listening_items.distractor_focus: 'for here' vs 'four here'; unreleased final /r/ and /k/ in 'to go' vs 'to go?'

listening_items.audio_text: Two large fries, one regular. No salt on the large ones.
listening_items.question: How many large fries, and what is the special request?
listening_items.answer: Two large fries; no salt on the large ones
listening_items.distractor_focus: fries vs fry; salt vs saw; large vs lard

listening_items.audio_text: Number ninety, your order's ready at counter four.
listening_items.question: Which number was called, and where do you collect?
listening_items.distractor_focus: ninety vs nineteen; four vs forty

listening_items.audio_text: Sorry mate, we're out of nuggets. Want chips instead?
listening_items.question: What is unavailable, and what is offered?
listening_items.answer: Nuggets are sold out; chips (fries) are offered
listening_items.distractor_focus: 'out of nuggets' — linked final consonants make the key word hard to catch

guided_roleplay.learner_role: Customer ordering a combo at a fast-food counter, with on-screen frames and a hint button
flow: Step 1 — Open the order: greet and say what you want ('Hi, can I get…?').
Step 2 — Answer the size question: choose small, medium or large clearly.
Step 3 — Customise: ask for one change (no ice / no onions / extra sauce).
Step 4 — Answer 'For here or to go?' in three words or fewer.
Step 5 — Handle the money: hear the total, check it if unsure ('Sorry, thirteen or thirty?'), say card or cash.
Step 6 — Collect: catch your order number and confirm the bag ('Did you get the water?').
sentence_frames: To go, please. / For here, thanks.

free_roleplay.ai_persona: A friendly but rushed fast-food cashier at lunchtime. Speaks quickly, uses short chunks ('What can I get you?', 'Size?', 'For here or to go?'), never uses names, and moves the queue along. Repeats once if asked, slightly slower.
free_roleplay.a2_behavior: Stays on the standard script: takes the order, asks size, asks for here or to go, gives a clear total and an order number, waits for the learner to finish each turn.
b1_curveballs: The item the learner ordered is sold out — offers an alternative the learner must ask about.
Upsells: 'Make it large for a dollar fifty more?' — the learner must accept or refuse politely.
Says the total fast and quietly, forcing the learner to ask 'Sorry, did you say thirty or thirteen?'
Asks an unexpected question: 'Any sauce with that?' or 'Is that a meal or just the burger?'
Hands over the bag with one item missing — the learner must notice and say so ('Sorry, I ordered a water too.').
The card machine fails: 'Sorry, cash only right now.'

roleplay_rubric.criterion: Placed a complete order: item + size + (drink or side) without the AI having to guess
Answered 'For here or to go?' correctly and audibly
Made at least one customisation request ('no ice', 'no onions', 'extra sauce')
Understood the total and the order number, or asked a clarification question to check them
Kept register casual-polite: used 'please'/'thanks', short turns, no over-formal phrasing
Pronunciation: final consonants audible in 'large', 'no ice', 'fries', 'to go'; teen/ty numbers distinguishable
Coped with an off-script problem (sold-out item, upsell, missing item, cash only) and finished the order anyway

register_culture_note.en: Fast-food English is short, fast and casual. Staff use clipped chunks ('Size?', 'For here or to go?') and expect three-to-five-word answers. Politeness lives in one word — 'please' or 'thanks' — not in long sentences. Full formal sentences slow the queue and actually sound odd; a short 'A large combo, please' is perfect. Asking staff to repeat is completely normal, and asking about the price is normal too.

do_dont.avoid: 'No ice' said as 'no eye' (final /s/ dropped) — staff hear nothing and fill the cup with ice.
do_dont.prefer: Push the final /s/ out: 'no ICE-s', slightly longer than feels natural.

do_dont.avoid: 'Lar' for 'large' — the /dʒ/ disappears and you are served a small.
do_dont.prefer: 'Large, please' with the ending released, or say 'the big one' as a backup.
'The same, please' or 'One of those, please.'

do_dont.avoid: 'I want a burger.' — grammatical but sounds blunt at a counter.
Nodding when you did not catch the total, then handing over the wrong money.
do_dont.prefer: 'Sorry, did you say thirteen or thirty?'

do_dont.avoid: Saying 'thirty' with no stress difference from 'thirteen'.
do_dont.prefer: Stress the first syllable and stop: THIR-ty; stress the second and hold the /n/: thir-TEEN.

register_culture_note.thai_cultural_note: In Thailand a polite ending particle (ครับ/ค่ะ) carries the politeness, so a bare 'I want large' can feel complete to a Thai speaker — but in English the politeness has to move into the words themselves ('Can I get… please?'). The other real difference is asking staff to repeat: many Thai learners stay quiet to avoid causing trouble for a busy worker, but here saying 'Sorry, thirteen or thirty?' is expected, takes two seconds, and is far less trouble than a wrong order. Note too that 'no ice' is a normal and common request abroad — you do not need to explain or apologise for it.

can_do_checkpoints.statement: I can order a combo by name or by number and choose a size.
I can answer 'For here or to go?' and ask for one change, like 'no ice'.
I can understand the total and my order number, and ask to hear them again.
I can cope when an item is sold out, ask what an alternative is, and reorder.
I can politely refuse an upsell and check that nothing is missing from my bag.
My final consonants ('large', 'no ice', 'fries') and my teen/ty numbers are clear enough for a drive-thru speaker.

unlocks: Drive-thru Mode (speaker distortion added to the AI voice)
Sold Out! (random item removed from the menu mid-order)

sound_meters.display: Endings meter — tracks released finals in 'large', 'ice', 'fries', 'to go'
Teen/Ty meter — tracks thirteen/thirty, fifteen/fifty accuracy across totals and order numbers
